headline: How regenerative farming is moving from niche to mainstream
meta_description: With government backing and private investment flowing in, regenerative farming is scaling up in the UK—but public awareness still lags far behind.
summary_short: At the UK's Groundswell farming festival, experts revealed how nature-friendly agriculture is gaining traction through policy support and £1.3m in new funding.
body:
Regenerative farming—a method that restores soil health and works with nature rather than against it—is quietly becoming a priority for the UK government, major household brands, and a growing number of farmers. Yet despite 80% of farmers adopting or planning to adopt regenerative methods, only 30% of the UK public has even heard of the term. At Groundswell, the UK's annual regenerative farming festival held last month in the English countryside, experts gathered to discuss how to bridge this gap and get nature-friendly food onto supermarket shelves where it belongs.

Three concrete shifts are accelerating the movement. First, the government released the Farming Roadmap 2050—its first long-term agricultural strategy—which prioritises soil health, reduced chemical inputs, and biodiversity. Environment secretary Emma Reynolds attended Groundswell to emphasise that "nature-friendly farming" is not an alternative to productive farming, but its foundation. Second, regeneratively grown food is emerging as a counterweight to ultra-processed foods, which carry health and environmental risks. As global concerns mount over processed food's effects on obesity and ecosystems, more people are seeking alternatives—over 25% of people worldwide now limit their processed food intake. Third, and crucially, money is moving into the sector. The Sustainable Farming Incentive is expanding, while private institutions are stepping up: Wildfarmed has launched a £1.3m fund with Lloyds Banking Group specifically designed to address regenerative farming's biggest barrier—financial viability for farmers. HSBC UK has also widened access to its Sustainable Farming Pathway programme.

Yet experts caution that the real work lies ahead. As regenerative ingredients begin appearing in mainstream products—Nestlé now uses regeneratively grown wheat in KitKats—questions linger about whether this genuinely serves nature and health. What remains clear is that success requires all actors in the food system to support farmers equitably, through long-term contracts and shared risks, not burden them alone.
quick_facts: 80% of UK farmers adopted or plan to adopt regenerative farming methods
Groundswell festival held in English countryside last month
Wildfarmed and Lloyds Bank launched £1.3m regenerative farming fund
70% of UK public unfamiliar with regenerative agriculture term
Government released Farming Roadmap 2050 prioritising nature-friendly methods
